newsitem.title: UK: UK to introduce tougher competition law -officials.
newsitem.headline: UK to introduce tougher competition law -officials.

text.p: The Labour government plans to introduce a tougher competition law in its initial legislative programme for the next 18 months, officials said on Tuesday.

The programme, to be announced in a speech on Wednesday by head of state Queen Elizabeth, will include 22 definite bills plus four others that will be introduced if time permits. There will also be three white policy papers, officials said.

Blair will tell parliament when he opens a debate on the Queen's Speech on Wednesday that his Labour party ran for office as "New Labour" on a one-nation platform that reflected the people's priorities, and that is how he intends to govern.
"We are the people's government," Prime Minister Tony Blair intends to say, according to an aide.
Blair will argue that his government has hit the ground running, offering new energy and a sense of purpose since it was elected on May 1.
"People feel they have a government back, a government determined to serve them," Blair proposes to say.
Two education bills form the centrepiece of the legislative programme, constituting what Blair believes is the "most fundamental attack on underachievement since the war".
One of the education bills will reduce the size of primary school classes. The second will raise school standards.

Other bills promised in the Queen's Speech will ban all handguns in the wake of last year's Dunblane massacre and pave the way for referenda on the government's plans for a tax-raising parliament in Scotland and an assembly in Wales.
Among other planned bills, one will dismantle the internal market in the National Health Service introduced by the Conservatives.
Another will increase charges for use of the radio spectrum, a move affecting broadcasters, minicabs and mobile phone users and could initially raise one billion pounds for the Treasury.
The finance bill to implement Labour's pending maiden budget will make a start on the government's welfare-to-work bill, to be funded by a windfall tax on privatised monopolies.
No details were available about the new competition law, but Labour's election manifesto promised "a tough prohibitive approach to deter anti-competitive practice and abuses of market power".
